results.summary_before: Tiny Number Simon is a Simon-style digital memory game implemented in Wokwi. It uses eight active-high buttons as number inputs and a common-cathode 7-segment display to show the sequence and score. The game requires a slow or manually stepped clock and an active-low reset, with no microcontroller or external memory needed. The design is notable for its simple state-machine implementation and clear test procedure.

results.summary_before: This ASIC implements a 60 Hz grid-forming reference using a CORDIC-locked sine wave generator and a linear dump-load controller for micro-inverters. It includes PWM modulators for driving an H-bridge and dump FET, with ADC sampling for AC and DC voltage feedback. The design requires substantial external hardware including a grid-tied solar system, H-bridge, transformer, rectifier, and dump load. It is notable for its complex control loops and power electronics application.

results.summary_before: This is a 5V-compatible version of a single-port SRAM block with 128 words of 8 bits, directly connected to the Tiny Tapeout tile pins. It operates synchronously with read and write operations on the clock edge, including write-through behavior. The design is full-custom and also compatible with 3.3V, using standard design rules. Testing is done by performing writes and reads to verify data retention.

results.summary_before: This is an analog four-stage differential delay voltage-controlled oscillator that uses a comparator tapping two stages to produce four single-ended quadrature outputs at 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees. Its nominal target frequency is 240 MHz with an expected tuning range of roughly 120 MHz to 500 MHz, controlled by an analog control voltage. Testing requires a programmable precision voltage source and an oscilloscope to observe oscillation. The design is notable for providing quadrature phases from a compact analog VCO suitable for clock generation or PLL use.

results.summary_before: This Verilog design drives a VGA display to show the text "DESIGN YOUR OWN CHIP" using the Tiny VGA pinout at a 25.175 MHz pixel clock. It outputs two bits each of red, green and blue along with horizontal and vertical sync on the eight outputs. It is used by connecting a VGA display through a Tiny VGA Pmod, with no other external hardware required. The project is a simple demonstration of generating a VGA signal from a Tiny Tapeout design.

results.summary_before: This Verilog design is an 8-bit signed fused multiply-add unit that computes z = a*b + c with a 16-bit internal product and sum, outputting the low 8 bits of the result. It uses a two-phase streaming protocol in which a and b are captured on even cycles and c on odd cycles, producing one result every two cycles with no separate valid signal. It is verified with cocotb tests covering reset, corner cases, 2000 randomized triples against a Python reference, and back-to-back streaming, plus a plain Verilog self-checking testbench. No external hardware is required, and the design is notable for its compact streaming arithmetic datapath.
